reading.title: Four Prefixes That Unlock Law and History
reading.purpose: See how prefixes like contra-, circum-, retro-, and pre- clarify rules, timing, and cause.
paras: Read almost any civics article or court summary and four Latin prefixes appear again and again: contra- (against), circum- (around), retro- (back), and pre- (before). Each one acts like a built-in signpost. At a border port, customs agents search cargo for contraband, forbidden goods that are illegal to bring in or sell. When a new rumor spreads confusion, officials publish clear records to counteract its effect, pushing back against the error before it grows. Sometimes two witnesses offer contrary statements that point in completely opposite directions.

The prefix circum- points to what surrounds a situation. Judges study every circumstance—each surrounding fact or condition—before deciding a fair outcome. Clever rule-breakers sometimes try to circumvent a law, finding a sneaky way around the written rule without technically crossing its front door. Good lawmakers close those loopholes once they spot how people dodge them.

Time-based prefixes matter just as much in courts and history. In retrospect, looking back at an old crisis with hindsight, mistakes often seem obvious. Yet a fair legal system rarely makes a punishment retroactive, applying a brand-new penalty backward to actions that were legal before the law existed.

Finally, pre- points ahead. A newly elected mayor often learns from the successes and errors of her predecessor, the leader who held the office before her. Declaring victory before all ballots are counted is premature—happening too soon—while a missing signature on a petition can preclude a candidate from appearing on the ballot, preventing it altogether. Spotting these four prefixes turns dense legal language into plain, readable logic.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "circumvent" most nearly means
choices: to apply a brand-new penalty to events from the past
to find a clever or sneaky way around a written rule
to inspect every crate at a border port for illegal items
to step down from public office before an election ends
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines circumvent directly as "finding a sneaky way around the written rule."

qs.q: Which sentence explains why fair legal systems avoid applying new punishments to past actions?
choices: Time-based prefixes matter just as much in courts and history.
In retrospect, looking back at an old crisis with hindsight, mistakes often seem obvious.
Yet a fair legal system rarely makes a punishment retroactive, applying a brand-new penalty backward to actions that were legal before the law existed.
Spotting these four prefixes turns dense legal language into plain, readable logic.
qs.why: This sentence defines retroactive penalties and points out that the past actions were legal before the new law existed.

ev.text: Yet a fair legal system rarely makes a punishment retroactive, applying a brand-new penalty backward to actions that were legal before the law existed.

qs.q: What can happen if a candidate's petition is missing a required signature?
choices: It can preclude the candidate from appearing on the ballot at all.
It forces the candidate's predecessor to stay in office for another term.
It allows officials to count the ballots before election day arrives.
It turns the petition into contraband that customs agents must seize.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 states that "a missing signature on a petition can preclude a candidate from appearing on the ballot, preventing it altogether."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Customs agents and judges rarely agree on how modern laws should be written.
Knowing four common Latin prefixes helps readers decode legal and historical vocabulary.
Ballot counting should always wait until a mayor's predecessor reviews every petition.
Loopholes in written laws are impossible for lawmakers to close once they appear.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows how contra-, circum-, retro-, and pre- unlock exact meanings in civics, law, and history.

the leader who held the office before her
